source.title: Migratory bats respond to artificial green light with positive phototaxis

method: field experiment: alternating 10-minute periods of 520 nm light at a central pole with acoustic monitoring on three poles; paired nightly totals
conditions: Wild, free-flying bats migrating south along the Baltic coast at Pape Bird Ringing Station, Latvia, 14 nights from 18 August to 3 September 2015; no captive animals. Median increase in activity during light-on was 54% for Nathusius' bats (minimum -34%, maximum 550%) and 47% for Soprano bats. No side or order randomisation is described beyond the alternation.

source.title: Supplementation of Male Pheromone on Rock Substrates Attracts Female Rock Lizards to the Territories of Males: A Field Experiment

method: field experiment: paired plots, rocks painted with ergosterol in dichloromethane versus dichloromethane alone, repeated censuses
conditions: Wild, unmarked lizards at Alto del Telégrafo, Guadarrama Mountains, central Spain (about 1,900 m), May to June 2009. Twelve areas of 15 x 6 m each held two 2 x 2 m plots; one plot per area was randomly assigned to ergosterol (25 g/L in dichloromethane, painted on rocks with brushes; 100 cL of solution per plot) and the other to the dichloromethane control (n = 12 pairs). Seven censuses per day, one every 30 min; treatment applied on four days (27 May, 2 and 3 June, 11 June) plus an initial day. Females did not differ between plots in the initial census or on the first (P = 0.43) and second day (P = 0.99) and were more abundant in treated plots on the third and fourth day (P = 0.007 and P = 0.017); the treatment main effect on females was not significant (F1,11 = 3.36, P = 0.09) and day had no effect (F4,44 = 1.28, P = 0.29), while the treatment x day interaction was significant (F4,44 = 2.83, P = 0.037); 46 females were seen near males in treated plots against 10 in control plots (binomial P < 0.0001). Nulls: the experimental manipulation did not affect male density (P = 0.10) or subadult density (P = 0.54). Counts are relative densities, not individuals; the authors state the method only provided estimations of relative densities. Ergosterol is an applied dose on the rock, not an airborne concentration; the paper gives no natural ergosterol level on rocks or in male femoral secretions for comparison. Lizards were not marked, observer blinding to treatment is not reported, and how male territories were identified is not stated.
quote: In the field, we added ergosterol to rocks inside the territories of male lizards, and found that this manipulation resulted in increased relative densities of females in these territories.

source.title: Lamp-Lit Bridges as Dual Light-Traps for the Night-Swarming Mayfly, Ephoron virgo: Interaction of Polarized and Unpolarized Light Pollution

method: field experiment: LED torch beamed at the compensatory-flight swarm with a horizontally polarizing filter versus a depolarised filter, alternating, mayflies counted from photographs
conditions: Wild swarms over the Danube at Tahitótfalu, Hungary, 23, 24, 27 and 28 August 2013 (about 99% females in carcass samples). units: categorical (camera-trap detection rate at lured vs unlured stations; mixed-model coefficient)

source.authors: Dacyn Holinda, Joanna M. Burgar, A. Cole Burton
source.title: Effects of scent lure on camera trap detections vary across mammalian predator and prey species

method: field experiment: paired lured and unlured camera-trap stations, detection counts modelled with zero-inflated negative binomial GLMMs
conditions: Free-ranging mammals in Alberta, Canada, February to August in 2015 and 2016. 844 camera stations (404 lured, 440 unlured) at 247 sites, four Reconyx PC900 cameras per site about 600 m apart at the corners of a square, the cameras in the northeast and southwest corners lured with one tablespoon of O'Gorman's Long Distance Call (a skunk and musk blend) in a PVC tube staked 5 m in front of the camera and those in the northwest and southeast corners without (fixed corners, not randomised; the paper does not say whether unlured stations had an empty tube or stake, so a visual novel-object cue is not excluded, and does not state lure replenishment); data truncated to 120 days after deployment; events defined with a 30 min threshold to reduce the influence of animals investigating the lure; mammals were detected at 800 of 844 stations, with 7110 detections at lured and 7530 at unlured stations. Zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models with site as random effect; the authors assumed any lure effect lasted the full 120 days and removed zero-inflation from the wolf model. Per-species lured and unlured counts are not reported in the text read. Lure is a commercial product, not a defined compound. Same paper: predators as a group, large and small carnivores and fisher were detected more at lured stations; prey, small mammals and ungulates were not. Fisher: beta = 2.23 +/- 0.36 SE, z = 6.18, p < 0.001. Gray wolf: beta = -0.01 +/- 0.34 SE, z = -0.03, p = 0.973; Richardson's ground squirrel: beta = 0.00 +/- 1.14 SE, z = 0.00, p = 0.998; moose: beta = 0.07 +/- 0.15, z = 0.50, p = 0.621. The authors say the scent likely draws investigative predators into the detection area and can alter their movement, so detection is a detectability and movement outcome, not abundance.
quote: Scent lure significantly increased detections of predators as a group, including large and small carnivore sub-groups and fisher specifically, but not of gray wolf.

value: placing wolf urine did not significantly affect deer behavior in either the wolf-absent or the wolf-present area

source.authors: Hermine Annette Lisa van Ginkel, Christian Smit, Dries Pieter Jan Kuijper
source.title: Behavioral response of naïve and non-naïve deer to wolf urine

method: field experiment: camera traps at dispensers of wolf urine, water and all-purpose soap, Kruskal-Wallis tests
conditions: Free-ranging red deer, spring 2016, two case studies: Veluwezoom National Park, Netherlands (wolf-absent; 25 locations, 75 plots, 507 trapping days, 69 red deer visits) and Bialowieza Forest, Poland (wolf-present; 20 locations, 60 plots, 415 trapping days, 115 visits). Three treatments per location (wolf urine, water as no-scent control, lemon-scented all-purpose soap as unfamiliar-scent control), plots at least 50 m apart, the cue for each plot randomly assigned within a location, all three present at once, one camera per dispenser for seven days; only individuals present more than 4 s were scored. Wolf urine was bought from a company that collects urine from animals in game farms, zoos and preserves, via floor drains in the animal cages, and was some months old; each dispenser was a 30 ml plastic tube with two holes at the top, identical for all three scents, and 15 ml remained after seven days. Cameras differed between areas (Ecotone in the Netherlands, Bushnell Trophy Cam HD in Poland), 1 m high and 8 to 10 m from the dispenser; the two areas were not compared statistically. Videos within five minutes were grouped as one visit and only one individual per group visit was scored; calves were excluded and sexes pooled because numbers were low and unequal. Eighteen Netherlands locations lay within 200 m of each other and were reused at six-week intervals. Seasonal hunting takes place in both areas. Roe deer were excluded for too few visits, and fallow deer, present only in the Netherlands area, were also excluded, so the analysed deer are red deer in both areas. Contrary result: in Poland foraging time was lower on soap plots (H = 7.088, P = 0.029), with a non-significant trend to higher vigilance (P = 0.088); soap had no effect in the Netherlands. Vigilance on control plots was 20% in both areas. Nulls for wolf urine and both controls (Kruskal-Wallis, df = 2): Netherlands visitation frequency P = 0.953, visit length P = 0.657 (41.7 +/- 8 s), vigilance P = 0.707, foraging P = 0.606, sniffing P = 0.194, walking P = 0.638, running P = 0.739; Poland visitation frequency P = 0.926, visit length P = 0.303, sniffing P = 0.727, walking P = 0.413, running P = 0.285. Sudden rush was scored 8 times (wolf plot 4, soap 2, water 2) and not tested. The authors suggest the cue was not strong or widespread enough, and that deer may associate wolf urine with domestic dogs. A behavioural null does not show that the urine went undetected.
quote: Placing wolf urine did not significantly affect deer behavior in either the wolf-absent or the wolf-present area.
